In many countries where English is not the first language, more and more universities teach their courses in English. I believe this is a positive development, although it can be difficult for some students.

The first advantage is that English is the international language of science and business. Most important research papers, books and websites are written in English, so students who study in English can read them easily. Also, when they graduate, they can work for international companies or find a job in other countries, because their English level is high. This give them a big advantage in the job market.

Another advantage is that universities can attract students and teachers from other countries. For example, a university in Asia which teach in English can accept students from Europe, Africa and South America. This makes the university more international, and local students can learn about different cultures and make friends from around the world. The university also earn more money from international students.

However, there are some problems. Some students have low level of English, so they cannot understand the lectures well, and their marks may be worse. In addition, if all courses are in English, the local language may become less important, especially in science subjects, and in the future there may be no modern textbooks in the local language at all.

In conclusion, I think teaching university courses in English is mostly a positive development because it helps students to find better jobs and make universities more international. But universities should give extra English classes to students who need it, so nobody is left behind.

samples.text:
Universities in many non-English-speaking countries are increasingly offering degree programmes taught entirely in English. Although this policy raises concerns about the quality of learning and the status of national languages, I consider it a positive development overall.

The main argument in its favour is that it prepares graduates for an international labour market. English is the dominant language of academic research, technology and global business, so students who have studied their subject in English are able to read the latest publications, attend international conferences and work confidently with colleagues from other countries. For a young engineer or economist, this can open up career opportunities that would otherwise be unavailable.

Teaching in English also allows universities to become more international. Courses in the local language are only accessible to local students, whereas English-medium programmes can attract applicants and academic staff from around the world. This diversity enriches the learning environment, as students are exposed to a wider range of perspectives, and it also bring valuable income from tuition fees.

Nevertheless, the trend is not without disadvantages. Students whose English is weak may understand only part of their lectures, and some lecturers may struggle to explain complex ideas in a second language, which could lower the standard of teaching. There is also a risk that the national language gradually loses its role in academic life, particularly in scientific fields. These problems, however, can be reduced by providing language support and by continuing to offer some courses in the local language.

In conclusion, while English-medium teaching presents certain challenges, it gives students valuable skills and helps universities compete globally. For these reasons, I regard it as a largely positive development.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · main ideas extended with relevant support · drawbacks acknowledged with solutions · clear paragraph topics and varied cohesion · good academic vocabulary · mostly accurate with a minor slip.

samples.text:
In a growing number of countries where English is not the native language, universities are replacing instruction in the national language with English, particularly at postgraduate level and in scientific and business disciplines. Although the motives behind this shift are understandable, I believe that, as it is currently being pursued, it is more negative than positive.

The rationale is clear enough. English has become the principal language of international scholarship and commerce, and graduates who can operate in it enjoy a significant advantage. English-medium programmes also enable universities to recruit international students and staff, raising their global profile and generating income from fees.

The first problem, however, is educational. Learning a demanding subject is challenging enough in one's first language; doing so through a language in which one is less than fluent inevitably consumes cognitive effort that would otherwise go into understanding the material. Students may memorise terminology without grasping underlying concepts, while lecturers who are not fully confident in English may simplify their explanations or avoid spontaneous discussion. The result can be a degree that sounds international but conveys less knowledge.

A second concern is the long-term impact on national languages. When advanced study and research are conducted exclusively in English, the local language ceases to develop the vocabulary needed for specialised fields. Over time, it risks being confined to everyday use, and knowledge becomes less accessible to citizens who do not speak English well. This also tends to favour students from wealthier backgrounds, who are more likely to have received strong English tuition at school.

In conclusion, while proficiency in English is undeniably valuable, making it the sole medium of university teaching can undermine both learning and linguistic heritage. Strengthening English as a subject, while teaching most courses in the national language, would achieve the benefits without these costs.
samples.why: Clear, well-argued negative judgement · opposing rationale fairly presented · ideas developed with insight into learning and language policy · skilful cohesion · precise academic vocabulary · error-free, varied structures.
